Name: CSV
Description: A comma separated value (CSV) file is a text file representing tabular data where each row is on a separate line and each column is separated by some delimiter character, usually a comma.

Share.explanation: CSV files are good for sharing data because they are usable by anything that can read a text file, including people. Encoding geometry other than points can be difficult, however, due to the difficulty of representing multiple vertices concisely.

Name: GeoJSON
Description: GeoJSON is structured text format that meets the GeoJSON standard for simple features, attributes, and collections of geometries.

Share.explanation: GeoJSON is good for sharing data because JSON is native to the browser. GeoJSON is a Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) standard format for geospatial data exchange and many applications are designed to parse it correctly. But it does get slow for datasets with lots over vertices.

Name: KML / KMZ
Description: Keyhole Markup Language (KML) is a type of XML file for storing feature geometry, attributes, and styling. KMZ is a zipped collection of KML files. The format was originally designed for Google Earth, but has since become an OGC standard.

Share.explanation: KML/KMZ files are usable for sharing data with Google Earth and some drone platforms that expect this format. GIS platforms can typically import, export, and display KML/KMZ files, but not use them directly for editing or analysis.

Display.explanation: KML/KMZ files are usable for display because they contain XML tags for styling. But the options are limited and can be difficult to use.

Name: GPX
Description: GPS Exchange Format (GPX) is type of XML file of waypoints in space-time, routes (collections of waypoints) and tracks (collections of routes). Some platforms extend the format to include attributes for each waypoint, route, or track.

Share.explanation: GPX files are usable for sharing data between GPS units and GIS platforms. GIS platforms can typically import and export GPX files, but frequently will not be able to visualize, edit, or use them in analysis directly.

Name: DWG / DXF
Description: DWG (drawing) and DXF (Drawing Exchange Format) are file formats for storing geometry, attributes, and metadata. DWG files are binary, and while DXF files can be ASCII text, they use encoded data that is not human-readable. Both formats are used for CAD systems and are largely controlled by Autodesk.

Share.explanation: DWG / DXF files are usable for sharing data between CAD and GIS platforms. GIS platforms can typically import, export, and view these files, but use the directly for editing or analysis.

Name: Shapefile
Description: A shapefile is several files that together represent a spatial dataset. It requires a .shp for the feature geometry, a .shx for the index, and a .dbf for the non-spatial attributes. A shapefile can include optional files like a .prj for the projection, .cpg for character encoding, .sbn/.sbx for the spatial index, and .xml for metadata.

Share.explanation: Shapefiles are usable for sharing data with legacy systems that require a shapefile. Useless otherwise. A format so bad there's a whole webpage just for hating it: switchfromshapefile.org

Analysis.explanation: GeoParquet files are excellent for analysis because their column-oriented storage and extensive metadata make analysis queries much more efficient.

Share.explanation: GeoParquet files are excellent for sharing data between GIS platforms because they use sophisticated data compression algorithms to reduce file size.

Cloud.explanation: GeoParquet files are excellent for cloud native GIS because they can be stored cheaply in object storage like S3. Their column-oriented storage, metadata, and support for HTTP range requests enable efficient queries without a server

FlatGeobuf files are excellent for cloud native GIS because they can be stored cheaply in object storage like S3. Their Hilbert-curve indexing and support for HTTP range requests enable efficient bounding box queries without a server

Esri.explanation: Spatial SQLite, implemented as a mobile geodatabase, is good to use for offline data editing with ArcGIS Field Maps and for solo work in ArcGIS Pro.

Analysis.explanation: Spatial SQLite files are useable for analysis of small datasets. The lack of columnar storage or a sophisticated query optimizer, however, make them less good for large datasets.

Records.explanation: Spatial SQLite files are good as a system of record because they use indexing for fast individual record reads and have ACID-compliant updates.

Share.explanation: A GeoPackages is a type of spatial SQLite file that is excellent for sharing data across platforms because it is an OGC-standard that is supported by every professional GIS platform. This is as close as you can get to a 1:1 replacement for shapefiles.

Esri.explanation: File geodatabases are good to use in ArcGIS Pro because they are the default. Many other tools in the Esri ecosystem will accept a file geodatabase as input or produce one as output.

Analysis.explanation: File geodatabases are useable for analysis of small datasets within ArcGIS Pro. The lack of columnar storage or a sophisticated query optimizer, however, make them less good for large datasets.

Records.explanation: File geodatabases are good as a system of record within ArcGIS Pro. They use indexing for fast individual record reads and have ACID-compliant updates.

Share.explanation: File geodatabases are good to share across ArcGIS products because they are familiar. They require compression to share effectively, which makes them less convenient.

Services.explanation: File geodatabases are usable for read-only map services published to ArcGIS Server. But disk I/O limits their useability for service-based editing workflows.

Esri.explanation: MVT, implemented as a vector tile layer, is excellent to use in ArcGIS for static layers like basemaps. The official Esri basemaps use MVT.

Services.explanation: Supports static spatial visualization services from GeoServer and other open-source platforms
Can be served from an API endpoint, but is best designed for serverless architecture

Cloud.explanation: Can be stored cheaply in object storage and streamed serverless to web maps

Name: Spatial relational database
Description: Spatial relational database combining storage and compute

Esri.explanation: A spatial relational database, implemented as an enterprise geodatabase, is excellent to use with ArcGIS . An enterprise geodatabase adds schemas and stored procedures specific to ArcGIS to a spatial relational database. A relational store is a spatial relational database that holds data for hosted feature layers in ArcGIS Online and ArcGIS Enterprise.

Analysis.explanation: A spatial relational database is good for analysis because it has a sophisticated engine for optimizing queries with spatial predicates. The lack of columnar storage, however, slows down analysis of the very largest datasets.

Records.explanation: A spatial relational database is excellent for systems of record because it use robust indexing for fast lookups, ACID-compliant updates for safe updates, and archiving for viewing historic data. Enterprise geodatabases also use versioning for multi-user editing.

Services.explanation: A spatial relational database is excellent for exposing data as services because it is designed for multiple simultaneous connects. They support OGC WMS and WFS formats, and enterprise geodatabases likewise support ArcGIS map and feature services.

Cloud.explanation: A spatial relational database is good for cloud native GIS when deployed using a Database-as-a-Service (DBaaS). A DBaaS allows effectively infinite scaling and offloads maintenance tasks to the service provider.

Name: Graph database
Description: Graph databases are a type of NoSQL database that tracks entities and their relationships. Examples include Neo4j, ArangoDB, and AWS Neptune

Esri.explanation: Graph databases are used to support ArcGIS Knowledge graphs. While this is a relatively niche use case, it cannot be done without a graph database.

Analysis.explanation: Graph databases are good for analysis that can be modeled as a graph problem. While not a common GIS workflow, it is useful when entities have both a spatial and non-spatial relationship, such as supply chains.

Records.explanation: Graph databases make good systems of record for data that is best modeled as entities and relationships. The way they organize data means they typically have fast record access and ACID-compliant updates without needing indexing.

Services.explanation: Graph databases can be used to expose data as an ArcGIS Knowledge graph service.

Name: Document store
Description: A document store is a distributed NoSQL database for storing and indexing JSON documents. It can use spatiotemporal indexing to make it useful for GIS workflows. Examples include Elasticsearch and OpenSearch.

Esri.explanation: A document store, implemented as the spatiotemporal big data store, used for persisting real-time data in ArcGIS Enterprise. It is useful when the volume or velocity of data is too high for the relational store to handle effectively.

Analysis.explanation: Document stores with a spatiotemporal index are good for analysis that is based on search or aggregation. The sophisticated indexing makes it possible to return queries across billions of documents very quickly.

Services.explanation: Document stores are good for exposing data as services because querying these stores is generally done through REST web APIs by default.

Name: Cloud data warehouse
Description: A cloud data warehouse is an elastic query compute engine that accesses data in separate object storage. You pay-as-you-go for analysis instead of keeping a database running. Examples include Snowflake, Amazon Redshift, and Google BigQuery.

Analysis.explanation: Cloud data warehouses are excellent for analysis because they store data in a columnar format that is highly optimized for the service provider's specific query engine.

Cloud.explanation: Cloud data warehouses are excellent for cloud native GIS workflows because you can scale arbitrarily large without any idle resources. You only pay for the storage and compute you actually use
